analysis.one_liner: Breaks up digital advertising middlemen that control both sides of ad sales and auctions.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote: it sat in the Senate Judiciary Committee from March 2023 until the Congress ended, despite 11 bipartisan sponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar companies earning more than $20 billion a year in digital advertising from owning more than one piece of the ad pipeline — so Google could not simultaneously run the ad auction, sell ad space for websites, and buy ads for advertisers. Companies over $5 billion acting as middlemen would have to put their customers' interests first, disclose fees and bidding data, and face lawsuits from the Justice Department, state attorneys general, and private advertisers if they violate the rules. The bill never received a committee hearing or vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Advertisers — from small businesses buying online ads to large brands — would gain, because middlemen could no longer quietly profit from both sides of the same auction and would have to seek the best price for each customer. Online publishers, including news sites that depend on ad revenue, would keep more of the money advertisers spend. Smaller ad-tech companies would gain a chance to compete for parts of the ad pipeline that giant firms would be forced to sell off. Consumers benefit indirectly, since advertising costs are ultimately built into the prices of goods and services, and ad-funded websites and news depend on a competitive ad market.

how_it_helps.text: Companies with more than $20 billion in annual digital ad revenue could no longer own both an ad exchange (the auction marketplace) and brokerage tools serving buyers or sellers, ending the arrangement where one firm sits on every side of its own auction.

Ad brokerages with more than $5 billion in digital ad revenue would owe their customers a best-interest duty and a best-execution duty — meaning they must seek the most favorable terms available for each customer's transaction and put customers ahead of themselves.

Customers could demand detailed records of bids, fees, and how their orders were routed, and brokerages would have to publish quarterly public reports on their routing practices, making hidden middleman fees visible.

The Justice Department and state attorneys general could sue violators on behalf of harmed businesses, and large firms' customers could bring private suits for the greater of $1 million per month of violation or actual damages, with class-action waivers prohibited.
All records tied to a customer's order would remain the customer's property, and any information shared must be anonymized so it cannot be used to track individual web users.

analysis.who_pays: Large digital ad-tech companies — above all Google, the only firm known to operate across the entire pipeline — would bear the cost: they would have to divest parts of their ad business within a government-reviewed process, comply with transparency and record-keeping rules, and face statutory damages of up to $1 million per month for violations. Advertisers could face some short-term disruption if divestitures temporarily reduce how efficiently ads are matched, and the Justice Department would shoulder the cost of reviewing divestitures and enforcing the new duties.

drawbacks.text: The private right of action allows statutory damages of $1,000,000 for each month of a violation even without proof of actual harm, which could generate lawsuits far beyond the conduct the bill aims to fix.

Forced divestitures could break apart integrated ad tools that currently match ads efficiently; supporters would have to acknowledge that the one-year transition, government review of divestiture plans, and separation of buy-side and sell-side operations could disrupt how online ads are bought and sold, at least initially.

The $20 billion and $5 billion revenue thresholds apply the rules only to a handful of very large firms, leaving the rest of the industry untouched — a targeted design that critics could call regulation written around specific companies.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core fix — stopping one company from running the auction while also representing both the buyers and sellers in it — addresses a genuine structural conflict of interest in a market that touches nearly every website and every business that advertises online, and the transparency and best-interest duties would give advertisers and publishers real leverage for the first time. The main honest costs are transition disruption in a market where integration has some efficiency benefits, and a statutory-damages scheme ($1 million per month) that is blunt and could outpace actual harm. On balance the bill's benefits to the broader economy and the open web plausibly outweigh those costs, though the litigation provision would have benefited from calibration.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Mike Lee introduced the AMERICA Act on March 30, 2023, with 10 cosponsors split across both parties — 7 of 49 Senate Republicans and 3 of 48 Senate Democrats — including antitrust leaders like Amy Klobuchar and progressive senators like Elizabeth Warren.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee on the day of introduction.
No further action ever appears in the record: no hearing, no committee markup, no floor vote, through the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Google and the other large digital ad-tech companies came out ahead: their integrated ad businesses — which the bill would have forced apart — remained untouched because the bill never advanced past committee referral.

for.name: Mike Lee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited a bipartisan group of 10 cosponsors; as a senior Judiciary Committee member he was positioned to move it.

for.name: Amy Klobuchar
for.role: U.S. Senator (D-MN), lead Democratic antitrust voice on Judiciary
for.what_they_did: Original cosponsor of the bill, lending the committee's main Democratic antitrust advocate to a Republican-led measure.

for.name: 7 of 49 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill (Cruz, Rubio, Schmitt, Hawley, Kennedy, Graham, Vance).

against.name: Dick Durbin
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee hearing or markup; the record shows no committee action after referral for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Google
against.what_they_did: The company most exposed to the bill's divestiture requirements; it was widely reported to oppose and lobby against ad-tech breakup legislation.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan from day one — a Republican lead sponsor joined by 7 of 49 Senate Republicans and 3 of 48 Senate Democrats, spanning the party's left and right flanks — but the bill never reached any vote where party lines could be measured.

industries.industry: Big tech digital advertising platforms (notably Google)
industries.note: Companies over $20 billion in digital ad revenue would be barred from owning the exchange plus buy-side or sell-side brokerage tools, forcing divestiture of parts of the ad stack; Google is the firm whose business structure the bill most directly targets. Its interest in preserving the integrated stack runs against advertisers and publishers, who pay the layered middleman fees the structure enables.

industries.industry: Advertisers (brands and small businesses buying online ads)
industries.note: Buy-side brokers would owe them a best-interest and best-execution duty, plus full transparency into bids, routing, and fees, and a private right to sue — advertisers would keep more of every advertising dollar.
Sell-side brokers would owe publishers the same duties, and ending self-dealing in auctions would let publishers capture more of the revenue that funds free content and journalism.
Divested exchange and brokerage businesses would have to be sold to qualified buyers, opening space for smaller competitors to take over parts of the pipeline now dominated by one or two giants.
